Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Ana García's memories of her childhood home were a jumble of fragmented images and sounds. She recalled the acrid smell of sweat that clung to her father after he'd been drinking, the way it seemed to seep from his pores like a warning sign. As a detective, Ana had learned to trust her instincts, but as a child, she'd been powerless to stop the domestic violence that ravaged her family. The worst nights were when her parents' shouting matches escalated into physical fights. Ana would cower in her bedroom, her heart racing with every crash and thud. She remembers trying to cover her ears, but the sounds still seeped through – the slap of skin on skin, the splintering of furniture. Even now, as a grown woman, Ana's body recoils at the sound of shouting, transporting her back to those terrifying nights. As she grew older, Ana learned to cope with the trauma by numbing herself to her emotions. She avoided physical touch, even with loved ones, fearing it would unleash a torrent of feelings she couldn't control. Her partner, Carlos, had grown accustomed to giving her space, but Ana knew he didn't understand why she sometimes pulled away from him in bed. Ana's colleagues at the precinct saw her as tough and capable, but they didn't know about the secret rituals she'd developed to cope with her anxiety. At night, she'd wake up multiple times to check that all doors and windows were locked, that Carlos was safe beside her. She'd position herself near exits in crowded rooms, always on high alert for potential threats. The memories of those childhood nights lingered, refusing to be fully grasped. When Ana tried to recall the details deliberately, she found it difficult to access them – as if her mind had built a protective barrier around the pain. But when memories did surface, they came in vivid, disturbing flashes: her father's face twisted in rage, the sound of shattering glass. Ana's self-doubt had grown over time, fueled by the fear that she was somehow to blame for the violence she'd witnessed. She worried that her reactions – the startle response, the hypervigilance – meant she was losing her grip on reality. Her mind whispered cruel truths: You're not a good person; you're just pretending to be normal. One coping mechanism Ana had developed was self-harm distraction. When memories or anxiety overwhelmed her, she'd inflict physical pain on herself – a twisted way of grounding herself in the present. It was a secret she kept hidden from Carlos and everyone else, ashamed of this dark aspect of her psyche. As a detective, Ana was skilled at piecing together evidence and solving crimes. But when it came to her own life, she felt lost and fractured. The latest case she'd worked on – a brutal domestic violence incident – had brought all her emotions boiling to the surface. She couldn't shake the image of the victim's battered face, the haunted look in her eyes. Ana knew she needed help, but the thought of confronting her past terrified her. What if she lost control completely? What if Carlos left her because he couldn't handle the truth about her? As she sat in her therapist's office, Ana felt like she was teetering on a precipice – unsure whether she'd find solace or further chaos in the process of healing.
